items.question: What is the continuous power rating of each main AC generator, and what does it increase to for emergency operation?
options: 75 kva continuous, 90 kva for emergency operation
90 kva continuous, 75 kva for emergency operation
35 kva continuous, 45 kva for emergency operation
115 kva continuous, no emergency rating
items.explanation: The two main generators are oil-cooled, brushless units producing three-phase 400 Hz power, rated at 75 kva for continuous operation and 90 kva for emergency operation. (35/45 kva are the APU generator's ratings, not the main generators.)
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.I-2-1)

items.question: What is the APU generator's power rating for continuous use versus five-minute use?
options: 35 kva continuous, 45 kva for five minutes
45 kva continuous, 35 kva for five minutes
75 kva continuous, 90 kva for five minutes
25 kva continuous, 35 kva for five minutes
items.explanation: The air-cooled, brushless APU-driven auxiliary generator produces 115 vac three-phase 400 Hz power, rated at 35 kva for continuous use and 45 kva for five minutes.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.I-2-1)

items.question: Which electrical bus remains powered ('hot') regardless of the BATT switch position?
options: The battery utility bus
The battery hold-up bus
The dc essential bus
None — all buses are unpowered with BATT OFF
items.explanation: The battery utility bus is always hot regardless of BATT switch position; turning the BATT switch ON connects the rest of the battery buses if the battery is the only source of power.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.I-2-4)

items.question: If both main generators fail and the APU generator is supplying reduced power, which of the following is automatically load-shed?
options: Pilot and copilot windshield anti-ice, No. 1 engine anti-ice, and main/tail rotor blade de-ice
The dc essential bus and both primary dc converters
Both engine FADECs and the AFCS
The fuel boost pumps and fuel quantity indication
items.explanation: Because the APU cannot support all aircraft ac loads, automatic load shedding disables pilot/copilot windshield anti-ice, No. 1 engine anti-ice, main and tail rotor blade de-ice, the AVC system, and the second air conditioning compressor (if installed).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.I-2-7)

items.question: Which fuel tank supplies the APU, and does it also supply an engine?
options: The No. 1 tank supplies both the APU and the No. 1 engine
The No. 2 tank supplies both the APU and the No. 2 engine
A separate, dedicated APU tank supplies only the APU
Both tanks supply the APU equally via the crossfeed line
items.explanation: Fuel from the No. 1 tank supplies both the No. 1 engine and the APU; fuel from the No. 2 tank supplies only the No. 2 engine. This asymmetry matters when planning fuel balance and APU availability.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FUEL SYSTEM (p.I-7-1)

items.question: What does a SOV1 WRNG POSN or SOV2 WRNG POSN caution indicate?
options: The affected engine fuel prime shutoff valve does not match its commanded position (e.g. starter on with the valve closed, or starter off with the valve open)
The affected engine fuel filter is nearing bypass
The affected engine fuel tank quantity is below 215 pounds
The affected engine fuel crossfeed valve has frozen open
items.explanation: Each fuel prime valve is monitored by a position indicator; the SOV WRNG POSN caution illuminates when the valve doesn't match its commanded position — for example, engine starter on with the affected shutoff valve closed, starter off with the valve open, or the prime pump manually selected on with the valve closed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FUEL SYSTEM (p.I-7-1)

items.question: What is the purpose of the Inlet Particle Separator (IPS) in the engine's cold section?
options: It removes foreign particles from the air before it enters the compressor
It separates fuel from air prior to combustion
It cools the compressed air before it reaches the diffuser
It filters oil before it reaches the main bearings
items.explanation: The cold section includes the Inlet Particle Separator (IPS), which removes foreign particles from the air before it enters the compressor, protecting the engine from FOD and erosion.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-1)

items.question: How do the two FADEC channels (A and B) share control of an engine over time?
options: They take turns controlling the engine, swapping control after every engine shutdown; if a FADEC is degraded, the channel with the least faults takes control
Channel A always has primary control, with Channel B only as a hot standby
Both channels always control the engine simultaneously with no swapping
Control alternates every 30 seconds during flight regardless of faults
items.explanation: Each FADEC has two channels (A and B) that take turns controlling the engine, swapping control after every engine shutdown. In case of a degraded FADEC, the channel with the least faults takes control.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-3)

items.question: Besides a rapid Ng deceleration rate, what other single Ng criterion will cause the FADEC to declare an engine failure?
options: Ng below 55%
Ng below 70%
Ng below 90%
Ng below 100%
items.explanation: The FADEC uses two indications to determine an engine failure: Ng decreasing at a rate faster than the FADEC commands, or Ng going below 55%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-7)

items.question: What is the operational purpose of the 30-second, 2-minute, and maximum continuous OEI power ranges, respectively?
options: 30 second stops the initial descent and recovers Nr/airspeed; 2 minute allows climb away from threatening terrain; maximum continuous allows cruise to a safe landing zone
30 second is for cruise to a safe landing zone; 2 minute stops the initial descent; maximum continuous allows climb away from terrain
All three ranges serve the identical purpose of maximizing cruise range
30 second and 2 minute are identical; only maximum continuous differs, for landing only
items.explanation: After an engine failure, 30 second OEI power stops the initial descent and helps recover Nr and airspeed; 2 minute OEI power allows the aircraft to climb away from threatening terrain; maximum continuous OEI power allows the aircraft to cruise to a safe landing zone.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-7)

items.question: Under which condition will the FADEC automatically arm two-minute OEI power on the good engine without pilot action, aside from moving a throttle out of FLY?
options: When there is a torque split of more than 20% and the low engine is below 70% torque
Whenever Nr exceeds 104% momentarily
Whenever the collective is raised above the hover torque setting
Only when the pilot manually selects it — there is no other automatic case
items.explanation: The FADEC automatically arms one of the OEI limits in three cases: when one engine fails, the remaining engine automatically arms 30 second power; when one engine throttle is moved out of FLY, the good engine automatically arms two minute power; and if there is a torque split of more than 20% with the low engine below 70% torque, the good engine automatically arms two minute power.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-7)

items.question: With the AIR SRCE HEAT/START switch in the ENG position and the APU on, which source provides bleed air at low engine power settings?
options: The APU is used as the bleed air source at low power settings, while the engine takes over at high engine power settings
The engine is always the source regardless of power setting or APU status
The APU is used exclusively at all power settings whenever ENG is selected
Bleed air is unavailable at low power settings in the ENG position
items.explanation: In the ENG position, the system selects the higher-pressure bleed air source: if the APU is on, it supplies bleed air at low engine power settings, while the engine itself becomes the source at high engine power settings.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENGINE (p.I-8-3)

items.question: How are the No. 2 engine and APU fire compartments linked for fire protection?
options: Arming the No. 2 engine discharges the selected bottle into both the No. 2 engine and APU compartments, and arming the APU discharges into both the APU and No. 2 engine compartments
They are completely independent; arming one has no effect on the other
Arming the APU discharges into the No. 1 engine compartment instead of the No. 2
The link only works one way: arming the APU affects No. 2 engine, but not vice versa
items.explanation: The No. 2 engine and APU compartments are linked together for fire protection: when the No. 2 engine is armed, the selected fire bottle discharges into both the No. 2 engine and APU compartments, and when the APU is armed, the selected bottle discharges into both the APU and No. 2 engine compartments.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM (p.I-11-2)

items.question: When the FIRE EXTG switch is set to RESERVE for an armed engine, which compartment receives the discharge?
options: The opposite engine compartment's reserve container discharges into the armed engine's compartment
The same engine's reserve container discharges into its own compartment, identical to MAIN
The reserve position discharges into the APU compartment regardless of which engine is armed
RESERVE only arms the system without discharging anything
items.explanation: In the MAIN position, the No. 1 or No. 2 fire extinguisher container discharges into its own respective engine compartment. In the RESERVE position, the No. 1 or No. 2 container discharges into the opposite engine compartment via the crossfeed system.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM (p.I-11-2)

items.question: What triggers the crash-actuated fire extinguisher system, and what does it do?
options: An inertia switch senses a crash impact of 10 Gs or more and automatically fires both extinguishing containers into both engine compartments
It triggers at 10 Gs and discharges only into the APU compartment
It requires manual pilot activation even after a crash impact is sensed
It triggers only when the FIRE/ARM pushbuttons have already been pressed
items.explanation: An inertia switch hard-mounted to the airframe senses crash forces; upon a crash impact of 10 Gs or more, the switch automatically fires both extinguishing containers into both engine compartments, without requiring the FIRE/ARM pushbuttons to be pressed first.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM (p.I-11-3)

items.question: Why are the engine and APU fire detectors powered from the dc battery bus rather than a generator bus?
options: So fire extinguishing capability remains available through battery power any time the generators are not operating
Because the battery bus is the only bus with enough current capacity for the detectors
It is purely a legacy wiring choice with no operational significance
So the detectors can be tested only while on battery power during preflight
items.explanation: The No. 1 engine, No. 2 engine, and APU fire detectors all receive power from the dc battery bus through dedicated circuit breakers, ensuring fire extinguishing capability is available through battery power any time the generators are not operating.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM (p.I-11-2)

items.question: Besides backing up the No. 1 and No. 2 hydraulic systems, what else does the No. 3 hydraulic system power?
options: The landing gear, cargo ramp, and automatic recharging of the APU accumulator
The AFCS servo actuators exclusively
The main and tail rotor blade de-ice system
The engine FADEC hydraulic actuators
items.explanation: The No. 3 hydraulic system provides backup pressure to the No. 1 or No. 2 systems in the event of a failure, and also provides hydraulic power for the landing gear, cargo ramp, and automatic recharging of the APU accumulator.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.I-14-1)

items.question: Why do the hydraulic backup shutoff valves automatically close during engine start and shutdown?
options: To prevent unwanted shuttling caused by interaction between the two primary hydraulic systems and the No. 3 system
To conserve hydraulic fluid while the rotor is not turning
To allow the ground checkout pump to operate without interference
It is a manual pilot action, not an automatic function
items.explanation: Both backup shutoff valves automatically close during engine start and shutdown to prevent unwanted shuttling from interaction between the two primary hydraulic systems and the No. 3 system; the DCUs close them when the first engine exceeds 15% Ng during start, and reopen them once Nr exceeds 50%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.I-14-3)

items.question: How does the emergency flotation system's design sea state depend on aircraft weight?
options: At or above 18,590 pounds it is designed for mid sea state 5 (8-12 ft waves); below that weight, mid sea state 4 (4-8 ft waves)
At or above 18,590 pounds it is designed for sea state 4; below that weight, sea state 5
The design sea state is fixed at sea state 5 regardless of aircraft weight
Weight has no bearing on the flotation system's design sea state
items.explanation: At aircraft weights at or above 18,590 pounds (8,432 kg), the emergency flotation system is designed to keep the helicopter upright and afloat long enough to evacuate in mid sea state 5 (8-12 ft waves, 18-25 kt wind); below that weight, it is designed for mid sea state 4 (4-8 ft waves, 17-21 kt wind).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I (OPTIONS): EMERGENCY FLOTATION SYSTEM (p.I-18-1)

items.question: What redundancy is built into each of the three emergency float bags, and how many nitrogen bottles inflate them in total?
options: Each bag has two independent pockets so a single pocket failure still leaves sufficient buoyancy; four nitrogen bottles inflate all the floats (two forward, two aft)
Each bag has a single pocket with no redundancy; two nitrogen bottles inflate all the floats
Each bag has three independent pockets; six nitrogen bottles inflate all the floats
The floats share one common pocket across all three bags, inflated by a single nitrogen bottle
items.explanation: Each of the three float bags consists of two separate, independent pockets, so a single pocket failure still leaves the remaining pocket providing sufficient buoyancy for that section. Four nitrogen bottles inflate the floats: two forward bottles (each inflating one pocket of the left and right forward floats) and two bottles in the tail boom (each inflating one aft float bag pocket).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I (OPTIONS): EMERGENCY FLOTATION SYSTEM (p.I-18-1)

items.question: In the standard transport configuration, what is the maximum number of passenger seats allowed, and how many for Category B operations?
options: 19 passenger seats for transport configuration; 9 for Category B operations
24 passenger seats for transport configuration; 12 for Category B operations
19 passenger seats for both configurations
9 passenger seats for transport configuration; 19 for Category B operations
items.explanation: A maximum of 19 passenger seats is allowed in the transport configuration; Category B configuration is limited to a maximum of 9 passenger seats.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-2, I-1-4)

items.question: How much does an empty standard passenger seat weigh, compared to an empty observer or attendant seat?
options: 24 lb for a passenger seat; 32 lb for an observer/attendant seat
32 lb for a passenger seat; 24 lb for an observer/attendant seat
20 lb for a passenger seat; 20 lb for an observer/attendant seat
24 lb for a passenger seat; 24 lb for an observer/attendant seat
items.explanation: Each empty passenger seat weighs 24 lb; the empty observer and attendant seats each weigh 32 lb.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-2)

items.question: What indication comes on if an air stair door section is unlocked while on the ground, versus in flight?
options: DOOR OPEN advisory on the ground; DOOR OPEN caution in flight
DOOR OPEN caution on the ground; DOOR OPEN advisory in flight
No indication on the ground; DOOR OPEN caution in flight
MASTER WARNING on the ground; DOOR OPEN advisory in flight
items.explanation: If either air stair door section is unlocked while on the ground, the DOOR OPEN advisory illuminates. If either section is unlocked in flight, the DOOR OPEN caution illuminates instead.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum load the cargo ramp can support?
options: 500 lb
items.explanation: The cargo ramp is a hydraulically operated, electrically controlled platform that can support up to 1000 lb, and includes a roller assembly for loading or unloading palletized equipment.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-9)

items.question: What powers normal landing gear extension and retraction, and what is used for emergency extension?
options: Normal: utility hydraulic system; emergency: a self-contained nitrogen blowdown system per actuator
Normal: electric motors; emergency: a hand-crank system
Normal: the No. 1 hydraulic system; emergency: the APU hydraulic pump
Normal and emergency both use the utility hydraulic system
items.explanation: Normal landing gear extension/retraction uses hydraulic pressure from the utility hydraulic system (specifically the No. 3 hydraulic system supplying the actuators). Each actuator also has a self-contained nitrogen blowdown system for emergency extension, released via the EMER DN switch.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-15, I-1-16)

items.question: What does the HARD LANDING caution indicate, and what triggers it?
options: A shear fuse switch on a shock strut has activated, indicating the shear ring has yielded
The weight-on-wheels switch has failed
The landing gear failed to lock down
Tire pressure has dropped below limits
items.explanation: A shear fuse switch on each shock strut activates the HARD LANDING caution, indicating that the shear ring — a frangible element designed to absorb energy from a hard landing — has yielded.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-15)

items.question: Is the S-92 nose landing gear steerable?
options: No — it casters 360° and is non-steerable
Yes, via a nosewheel steering tiller
Yes, but only below 10 knots ground speed
It is steerable only when the parking brake is off
items.explanation: The nose landing gear wheel and tire assembly can caster a full 360° and is non-steerable.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-15)

items.question: Under what conditions does the LDG GEAR UP warning (and the EGPWS "Too Low Gear" aural warning) activate?
options: Airspeed below 60 KIAS and radar altitude below 150 ft AGL (100 ft AGL in EGPWS low altitude mode), with the gear not down
Airspeed below 100 KIAS at any altitude
Radar altitude below 500 ft AGL regardless of airspeed
Only when the collective is below a set position
items.explanation: Both the LDG GEAR UP master warning and the EGPWS "Too Low Gear" aural warning trigger when the landing gear is not down, airspeed is below 60 KIAS, and radar altitude is below 150 ft AGL (100 ft AGL if EGPWS is in low altitude mode).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-18)

items.question: On the ground, what does the weight-on-wheels (WOW) switch do to the TCAS?
options: Disables TCAS on the ground; enables it in flight
Enables TCAS on the ground; disables it in flight
No effect — TCAS is always enabled
Switches TCAS to standby only above 10,000 ft
items.explanation: The weight-on-wheels switch disables TCAS while the aircraft is on the ground, and enables it once airborne.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-17)

items.question: On the ground, the weight-on-wheels switch disables ATT (attitude) hold on the AFCS — but what does the display still show?
options: The ATT hold indicator still shows ON, even though the function is disabled
The display blanks completely
It shows a red X over the attitude indicator
It automatically switches to heading hold display
items.explanation: On the ground, the WOW switch disables ATT hold on the AFCS, but the ATT hold indicator on the display still shows ON — a detail worth knowing so it isn't mistaken for a fault.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-16)

items.question: What is the maximum weight the engine cowling platform is designed to hold for maintenance access?
options: 400 lb
150 lb
800 lb
250 lb
items.explanation: Each engine cowling serves as a platform for preflight inspection and engine maintenance, and holds a maximum of 400 lb.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-19)

items.question: What does the sliding fairing on top of the fuselage provide access to?
options: The forward main rotor pylon area, including trim actuators via a secondary access door
The tail rotor gearbox only
The APU compartment only
The nose landing gear bay
items.explanation: A sliding fairing allows access to the forward main rotor pylon area. When slid open, a sliding fairing access door additionally allows access to the trim actuators.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-19)

items.question: How many cabin emergency exits does the S-92 have, in addition to both pilots' windows and the air stair door's upper section?
options: Three
Two
Four
One
items.explanation: The S-92 has three cabin emergency exits, in addition to both pilots' windows and the upper section of the air stair door, which also serves as a cabin emergency exit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-10)

items.question: How are the pilots' windows jettisoned in an emergency?
options: By rotating the interior release handle aft, or pressing the red button and rotating the exterior release handle counterclockwise
By pulling a single red T-handle beside the seat
They cannot be jettisoned; only the cabin exits can
By breaking the glass with an emergency hammer
items.explanation: The pilots' windows can be jettisoned by rotating the interior emergency release handle aft, or from outside by pressing the red button and rotating the exterior release handle counterclockwise. The window is removed lower end first.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-10)

items.question: How can the S-92 be fueled, and when is the fuel system interconnecting line used?
options: By pressure or gravity fueling; the interconnecting line is used only during closed-circuit pressure fueling
By gravity fueling only; the interconnecting line is used at all times
By pressure fueling only; there is no interconnecting line
By pressure or gravity fueling; the interconnecting line is used only during gravity fueling
items.explanation: The helicopter can be pressure or gravity fueled. During gravity fueling, the tanks are serviced independently — the fuel system interconnecting line is used only during closed-circuit pressure fueling.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-20)

items.question: What material is used for the upper cowling area and horizontal stabilizer of the S-92 airframe?
options: Graphite and graphite honeycomb
Sheet aluminum with stringers and longerons
Acrylic plastic
Titanium alloy
items.explanation: The entire upper cowling area and horizontal stabilizer are constructed of graphite and graphite honeycomb, while the cabin/fuselage uses sheet aluminum with stringers and longerons for strength.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-4A)

items.question: What indication illuminates if the cargo ramp or cargo upper door is unlocked during ground operations, versus in flight?
options: RAMP OPEN advisory on the ground; RAMP OPEN caution in flight
RAMP OPEN caution on the ground; RAMP OPEN advisory in flight
No indication on the ground; MASTER WARNING in flight
DOOR OPEN advisory in both cases
items.explanation: If the cargo ramp or upper door is unlocked during ground operations, a RAMP OPEN advisory illuminates. If unlocked in flight, a RAMP OPEN caution illuminates instead.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-9)

items.question: Can the sliding upper door be combined with the standard lower air stair door for SAR operations?
options: The sliding upper door may be used with the standard air stair (lower) door, but SAR operations with that combination are not permissible
Yes, this is the standard configuration for all SAR operations
No, the two door types can never be combined on the same aircraft
Only during daytime operations
items.explanation: The sliding upper door may be used together with the standard lower air stair door; however, SAR operations using that particular combination (lower air stair door with upper sliding door) are not permissible.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AIRFRAME (p.I-1-9)

items.question: How long can the Helicopter Emergency Egress Lighting System (HEELS) operate underwater?
options: At least 10 minutes
At least 2 minutes
At least 30 minutes
It is not rated for underwater use
items.explanation: HEELS lights, which outline the cabin/cockpit emergency exits and push-out windows, are capable of operating underwater for at least 10 minutes and have a self-contained power supply.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-5)

items.question: How many external emergency lights are installed, and where?
options: Six: four near the main cabin emergency exits and two at the cargo ramp
Four: one at each cabin emergency exit only
Two: one at each side of the fuselage
Eight: two at each cabin exit
items.explanation: Six external emergency lights illuminate exit areas when helicopter electrical power is lost — four near the four main cabin emergency exits, and two at the cargo ramp.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-5)

items.question: How many anti-collision lights does the S-92 have, and where are they located?
options: Two: one on top of the tail pylon and one on the bottom of the fuselage
One, on top of the tail pylon only
Four: one on each sponson and two on the tail pylon
Two: one on each wingtip sponson
items.explanation: There are two anti-collision lights — one on top of the tail pylon, the other on the bottom of the fuselage. Both are red and can be either a rotating beacon or a strobe.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-6)

items.question: What are the colors and locations of the S-92's position lights?
options: Red on the left sponson, green on the right sponson, white on top of the tail pylon
Green on the left sponson, red on the right sponson, white on the nose
Red and green both on the nose, white on the tail
All white, one on each sponson and one on the tail pylon
items.explanation: Position lights are mounted outboard on the left (red) and right (green) sponson, and on top (white) of the tail pylon.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-6)

items.question: How many landing lights are fitted under the nose, and what is each rated at?
options: Two, each 450 watts
One, 900 watts
Two, each 250 watts
Four, each 200 watts
items.explanation: Two 450-watt landing lights are located under the nose of the helicopter.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-6)

items.question: Through what arc can the controllable searchlight pivot, and how is it controlled?
options: 0° (stowed) to 120° full forward, with 360° rotation, controlled from the collective stick grips
0° to 90°, controlled from the cyclic stick grip
A fixed position with no articulation, controlled from the console
0° to 180°, controlled by a floor pedal
items.explanation: The 450-watt controllable searchlight, mounted under the right nose, is controlled from either collective stick grip: the SRCHLT SLEW switch allows 360° rotation and varies the pivot angle from 0° (stowed) to 120° (full forward).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-6, I-3-7)

items.question: How many cabin emergency lights are there, and what powers the forward and aft lights?
options: Three lights, with the forward and aft lights each using separate emergency power supplies
Three lights, all sharing a single common emergency power supply
Six lights, powered only by the main aircraft battery
One light per exit, powered by the DC Essential bus
items.explanation: The three cabin emergency lights, located adjacent to the cabin dome lights, are controlled by the EMERG LTS CABIN switch. The forward and aft lights each use separate emergency power supplies.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-4)

items.question: What is the normal in-flight position for the cockpit emergency lighting switches, and why?
options: ARM — so the emergency power supplies automatically turn the lights on if aircraft power is lost
ON — so the lights are always illuminated during flight
OFF — to conserve the emergency battery
It doesn't matter, as the cabin panel always takes priority
items.explanation: Normally the cockpit emergency lighting control switches are set to ARM (with the cabin EMERGENCY LIGHTS panel switches OFF), so the emergency power supplies automatically activate the lights if helicopter power is lost.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-4)

items.question: What does the rotor head inspection light illuminate, and for whom?
options: The main rotor droop stops, for ground personnel
The tail rotor gearbox, for maintenance crew in flight
The main rotor blades in flight, for the pilot
The engine intakes, for ground personnel
items.explanation: The rotor head inspection light illuminates the main rotor droop stops for ground personnel; it's mounted on the main rotor fairing, forward and to the right of the transmission.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-7)

items.question: Where does the cargo load light illuminate?
options: The area beneath the tail cone and immediately aft of the cargo ramp
The cabin interior directly above the cargo hook
The area forward of the nose gear
The main rotor pylon area
items.explanation: The cargo load light illuminates the area beneath the tail cone and immediately aft of the cargo ramp, controlled by the CARGO LOAD switch (with a CREW position that transfers control to the ramp control panel).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-6)

items.question: What does moving the P/B LAMP TEST switch to TEST verify in the cockpit?
options: That AFCS pushbuttons, fire extinguisher test indicators, landing gear position indicators, master warning indicators, and engine/APU ARM pushbuttons illuminate (plus optional equipment if installed)
Only the master warning panel bulbs
Only the landing gear position lights
The entire electrical system's circuit breakers
items.explanation: The P/B LAMP TEST switch tests all cockpit pushbutton and indicator lights: AFCS pushbuttons, fire extinguisher test indicators, landing gear position indicators, master warning indicators, engine and APU ARM pushbuttons, standby instrument EMER PWR and BATTERY TEST pushbuttons, plus optional equipment (weather radar, life raft, flotation, ELT, hoist) if installed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-2)

items.question: Turning on the FASTEN SEATBELTS or NO SMOKING cabin lights also does what else?
options: Activates the cabin alerting system's voice recording for that announcement
Automatically dims all cabin overhead lights
Triggers a chime in the cockpit only
Locks the cargo ramp closed
items.explanation: Turning on the FASTEN SEATBELTS and/or NO SMOKING lights also activates the appropriate cabin alerting system voice recording, in addition to illuminating the passenger advisory light.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: LIGHTING SYSTEMS (p.I-3-3)

items.question: What are the main components of the Avionics Management System (AMS)?
options: Four MFDs (optional fifth), two Display Control Panels, two Data Concentrator Units, and one Maintenance Data Computer
Two MFDs, one DCP, one DCU
Six MFDs and a single central processor
One MFD per pilot and a shared FMS only
items.explanation: The AMS consists of four Multi-Function Displays (an optional fifth is available), two Display Control Panels (DCPs), two Data Concentrator Units (DCUs), and a Maintenance Data Computer (MDC).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-1)

items.question: On power-up, what display mode does each MFD default to?
options: Outboard MFDs default to PFD, inboard MFDs default to EICAS, the center MFD defaults to NAV
All MFDs default to PFD
Outboard MFDs default to NAV, inboard MFDs default to PFD
All MFDs default to EICAS until manually changed
items.explanation: When power is first applied (or after being off for one second or more), the outboard MFDs default to PFD, the inboard MFDs default to EICAS, and the center MFD defaults to NAV display.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-1)

items.question: If one MFD fails, what happens to the other MFD on that same side of the instrument panel?
options: It automatically reverts to full-format PFD; the mode can be manually changed 2 seconds after the reversion
It also fails, requiring both to be reset
Nothing changes automatically; the pilot must manually select PFD
It switches to EICAS automatically and cannot be changed
items.explanation: If a display fails, automatic reversion forces the other MFD on that side of the instrument panel to full-format PFD. The display and format can then be manually changed two seconds after the automatic reversion takes place.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-1)

items.question: What are the three MFD built-in-test (BIT) types, and when does each run?
options: PBIT (power-up, runs at turn-on), CBIT (continuous, runs while operating), IBIT (initiated, runs when the operator triggers it)
PBIT, CBIT and IBIT all run continuously and cannot be triggered manually
There is only one BIT type, which runs once per flight
PBIT (pilot-initiated), CBIT (crew-initiated), IBIT (inspector-initiated)
items.explanation: The Power-up built-in-test (PBIT) runs each time an MFD is turned on; the Continuous built-in-test (CBIT) runs continuously while the MFD is operating; the Initiated built-in-test (IBIT) runs when initiated by the operator.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-1)

items.question: What is the difference between an "MFD Fail" and an "MFD Degraded" condition?
options: MFD Fail means data may be incorrect or misleading and is removed; MFD Degraded means normal operation continues with all valid data retained
They mean the same thing, just different labels
MFD Fail is a cosmetic issue only; MFD Degraded means the display is completely blank
MFD Degraded is more severe than MFD Fail
items.explanation: MFD Fail means the fault could allow incorrect or misleading data, so that data is removed from display and other MFDs are notified. MFD Degraded means normal operation is not prevented — the display retains all valid data and simply flags data affected by the fault.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-1, I-4-2)

items.question: In the Display Control Panel's master/slave arrangement, which display is always the "master"?
options: The outboard display — it computes new values for DCP inputs and sends them to the inboard display
The inboard display
Whichever display the pilot last touched
The center MFD
items.explanation: The outboard display is always designated the master: it computes new values for each DCP input and sends them to the inboard display. If the inboard display stops receiving that data, it computes its own values from the DCP inputs directly.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-2)

items.question: How many Data Concentrator Units (DCUs) are required for all MFD displays to remain available?
options: Only one — the DCUs operate independently
Both are required at all times
None — MFDs can operate with zero DCUs
Three of the four MFDs must have a working DCU
items.explanation: The pilot's and copilot's DCUs operate independently, and only one is required for all MFD displays to be available. If a DCU fails, the affected data is replaced by red dashes and a DCU1 or DCU2 annunciation appears on all EICAS pages.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-3)

items.question: How long does the AHRS ground alignment normally take, and when is a temperature stabilization phase added?
options: 30 seconds normally; an additional ~25 seconds if OAT is below +15°C or above +35°C
5 seconds normally, with no temperature-dependent extension
2 minutes normally, reduced in cold weather
It takes as long as the engine start sequence and cannot be timed separately
items.explanation: After applying power, the AHRS automatically performs a 30-second ground alignment during which the helicopter must not be moved. If OAT is below +15°C or above +35°C, a temperature stabilization phase is added that could last an additional 25 seconds.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-4)

items.question: If the AHRS needs to perform an in-flight alignment after a power interruption, what must the pilot do?
options: Fly straight and level for at least 120 seconds (possibly longer in turbulence)
Enter a standard rate turn for 60 seconds
Descend below 500 ft AGL until alignment completes
Nothing — in-flight alignment is not possible and a full landing is required
items.explanation: During an in-flight AHRS alignment, the aircraft must be flown straight and level for a period of at least 120 seconds; in turbulent air, alignment may take longer even while flying straight and level.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-4, I-4-5)

items.question: On the DCP's REF SET control, which parameter is the one exception that each pilot must set independently rather than it adjusting both sides at once?
options: BARO (barometric altimeter setting)
ALTP (altitude preselect)
MIN (minimum barometric altitude)
RA (radar altitude alert)
items.explanation: With the exception of BARO, each REF SET knob adjustment updates both sides of the cockpit. BARO is the one exception — each pilot must set his own altimeter independently.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-5)

items.question: What is the difference between a DCP "degraded" flag and a DCP "failed" flag?
options: Degraded means the onside displays don't agree with each other; failed means the displays aren't receiving data from the DCP at all
They are the same condition, shown with different colors
Degraded is worse than failed
Failed only applies to the pilot's DCP, degraded only to the copilot's
items.explanation: A DCP is "degraded" when the information received from the onside displays does not agree; a DCP is "failed" when the displays do not receive any data from the DCP at all.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-6)

items.question: What do the hook buttons on the hand-grip slew controllers do?
options: Transfer the current cursor position to the FMS, establishing a temporary waypoint
Lock the cursor in place on the MFD
Switch the display between PFD and NAV modes
Silence the current aural alert
items.explanation: The slew button moves the cursor on the MFD like a computer mouse; pressing any of the three hook buttons sends the current cursor location to the FMS, establishing a temporary waypoint.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-6)

items.question: What four PFD display formats are available, selectable from any other PFD format?
options: Full rose HSI, HSI arc, Composite, and Category A
PFD, NAV, EICAS, and HLTH only
Day, Night, Dusk, and NVG modes
Full, Half, Quarter, and Minimized
items.explanation: The four PFD formats are Full rose HSI ("FULL"), HSI arc ("ARC"), Composite ("COMP"), and Category A ("CAT A"), each selectable via a soft bezel key.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-7)

items.question: On the PFD attitude display, what do the black and magenta symbols represent?
options: Black shows actual aircraft attitude; magenta shows the flight director's commanded/requested attitude
Black shows commanded attitude; magenta shows actual attitude
Black is for the pilot's side, magenta for the copilot's side
Both colors show actual attitude, just from different sensors
items.explanation: On both the Single Cue and Cross Pointer symbology, the black symbol represents actual aircraft attitude while the magenta symbol represents the flight director's requested/commanded attitude — the FD command is satisfied when the two are aligned.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-8)

items.question: At what pitch and roll thresholds does the PFD shift to a de-cluttered "unusual attitude" display mode?
options: Pitch greater than +30° or less than -20°, or roll angle greater than ±65°
Pitch greater than +10° or less than -10°, or roll greater than ±30°
Only on roll exceeding ±90°, regardless of pitch
Only during autorotation, regardless of attitude
items.explanation: When pitch exceeds +30° or is less than -20°, or roll angle exceeds ±65°, the PFD shifts to a de-cluttered display, removing items like flight director cues, airspeed/altitude reference bugs, and deviation scales. Full information returns once pitch is back within -15° to +25° and roll is back within ±60°.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-11, I-4-12)

items.question: What does the red hash mark at 120 KIAS on the airspeed indicator denote?
options: The maximum speed for autorotation, single engine, and SAS-off operation
The never-exceed speed (Vne) for all configurations
The minimum speed for safe autorotation entry
The maximum speed for external load operations
items.explanation: A hash-marked red line at 120 KIAS on the airspeed indicator denotes the maximum speed for autorotation, single engine operation, and SAS-off operation.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-13)

items.question: If ADC airspeed data becomes unavailable, how can indicated airspeed be restored to the display?
options: By using the ADC switch on the reversionary panel
By recycling the MFD power
It cannot be restored until landing
By switching to the standby/backup airspeed indicator, which permanently replaces the primary display
items.explanation: If an ADC input becomes unavailable, the airspeed pointer and digital readout are replaced by an "IAS" flag. Airspeed indication can be restored by using the ADC switch on the reversionary panel to select the other (functioning) ADC.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-13, I-4-14)

items.question: What two aircraft parameters does the ADC use to continuously compute Vne?
options: Gross weight and density altitude
Outside air temperature and rotor speed only
Fuel quantity and torque
Pressure altitude and true airspeed
items.explanation: The ADC continuously computes the Vne value based on the aircraft's gross weight and density altitude; a red arc on the airspeed scale shows the Vne region, and the pointer/readout turn red if Vne is exceeded.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-13)

items.question: What is the function of the BRG 1 and BRG 2 knobs on the Display Control Panel?
options: They select the navigation source (ADF, VOR/NAV, or LNAV/FMS) for the #1 and #2 bearing needles on the PFD and NAV page
They set the barometric pressure reference for each pilot
They control MFD screen brightness
They toggle between metric and imperial units
items.explanation: The BRG 1 and BRG 2 knobs select the navigation source for the #1 and #2 bearing needles: ADF selects the Automatic Direction Finder, NAV selects the VOR receiver, and LNAV selects the onside FMS (if two FMS are installed).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-5)

items.question: How is reversion accomplished when one of the redundant AHRS, DCU, or ADC systems fails or becomes unreliable?
options: By moving the affected system's reversion switch out of NORM and selecting the functioning side, so it provides data to both sides of the cockpit
The system reverts automatically with no pilot action possible
By pulling the affected system's circuit breaker
By restarting the affected MFD
items.explanation: Reversion control is provided for the redundant AHRS, DCU and ADC systems. If one fails or becomes unreliable, the pilot moves that system's reversion switch out of NORM and selects the functioning side, so it supplies single-source data to both sides of the cockpit — annunciated on each PFD.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AVIONICS MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (p.I-4-3)

items.question: What does the RTU's IDENT key do?
options: Causes an ATC identification pulse to be transmitted by the transponder, with a blue-green ID shown on the RTU display
Identifies which radio is currently active on the display
Runs a self-test of the RTU processor
Switches the RTU to cross-side tuning mode
items.explanation: The IDENT key causes an ATC identification pulse to be transmitted by the transponder; when pressed, a blue-green ID indication appears on the RTU display confirming the pulse was sent.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-1, I-5-2)

items.question: What does the DME-H key on the RTU do?
options: Toggles DME hold, decoupling the DME frequency from the VOR/ILS frequency so a new VOR/ILS frequency can be selected without detuning the DME
Holds the current COM frequency and prevents any changes
Switches the DME to a backup antenna
Mutes the DME audio identification tone permanently
items.explanation: The DME-H key toggles DME hold on or off. When hold is active, the DME frequency is decoupled from the VOR/ILS frequency, so a new VOR/ILS frequency can be tuned without affecting the held DME frequency (shown in green followed by a yellow H).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-2)

items.question: On the RTU's color convention, what does magenta indicate?
options: A control fault for that radio from that RTU — if both RTUs show magenta, the radio itself has failed
The radio is actively transmitting
The radio is tuned to an emergency frequency
The radio is in cross-side tuning mode
items.explanation: Magenta on one RTU indicates a control fault for that radio from that particular RTU. If both RTUs display magenta for the same radio, this indicates the radio itself has failed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-2)

items.question: If both RTUs try to command the same radio simultaneously, which one takes precedence?
options: The pilot's RTU
The copilot's RTU
Whichever RTU issued the command first
Neither — the command is rejected and an error page is shown
items.explanation: When both RTUs attempt to command the same radio simultaneously, the pilot's RTU takes precedence.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-3)

items.question: If an RTU fails, how does the pilot enable "reversionary tuning" to control the cross-side radios from the working RTU?
options: Turn the failed RTU off, then push the 1/2 function key on the onside (working) RTU
Pull the circuit breaker for the cross-side radio
Reversionary tuning happens automatically with no pilot action
Press IDENT twice on the working RTU
items.explanation: To select reversionary tuning, turn the failed RTU off using its brightness/on-off knob, then push the 1/2 function key on the onside RTU. The failed RTU should remain off for the rest of the flight.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-3)

items.question: In cold weather, how does the RTU's power-up delay behave below −20°C?
options: 1 minute of additional power-up delay for each degree below −20°C, up to a maximum of 10 minutes
A fixed 4-second delay regardless of temperature
The RTU will not power up at all below −20°C
5 minutes of delay regardless of how cold it is
items.explanation: Between −20°C and +70°C, the RTU powers up normally with just a 4-second delay. Below −20°C, there is an additional 1-minute power-up delay per degree below −20°C, up to a maximum of 10 minutes; full display brightness may take up to another 10 minutes after that.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-4)

items.question: On the cyclic PTT (push-to-talk) trigger switch, what is the difference between the first and second detent?
options: First detent transmits over the ICS; second detent transmits over the selected radio
First detent transmits over the selected radio; second detent transmits over the ICS
Both detents do the same thing for redundancy
First detent is for the pilot, second detent is for the copilot
items.explanation: The cyclic PTT is a two-position trigger switch: pressing it to the first detent transmits over the ICS, while pressing it to the second detent transmits over a selected radio.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-5)

items.question: What does the EMER switch on the No. 1 audio controller do when pushed down, and on which controller is it disabled?
options: Connects the copilot's headset to the No. 1 radio regardless of other panel settings, cutting that station off from the ICS; the switch is disabled on audio controller No. 3
Broadcasts a MAYDAY call automatically on all radios; disabled on controller No. 2
Silences all audio to the affected station; disabled on controller No. 1 itself
Switches all radios to the emergency frequency 121.5 MHz; not disabled on any controller
items.explanation: Pushing EMER on the No. 1 audio controller connects the copilot's headset directly to the No. 1 radio regardless of other settings (the equivalent switch on the No. 2 controller connects the pilot to the No. 2 radio). While EMER is selected, that station cannot hear or be heard on the ICS. This switch is disabled on audio controller No. 3.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-5)

items.question: In what frequency increments can the VHF-422D COM radio be tuned, and where does the finer increment apply?
options: 25 kHz across the full range, or 8.33 kHz — but only from 118.00 to 136.990 MHz
8.33 kHz across the entire range with no restriction
50 kHz only, with no fine-tune option
25 kHz below 130 MHz, 8.33 kHz above 130 MHz
items.explanation: The COM can be tuned in 25 kHz increments between 118.00–151.975 MHz, or in 8.33 kHz increments only between 118.00–136.990 MHz — 8.33 kHz operation is not permitted above 136.990 MHz.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-7)

items.question: Which COM preset is permanently programmed to the emergency frequency, and what is that frequency?
options: Preset 20, at 121.5 MHz
Preset 1, at 121.5 MHz
Preset 10, at 123.45 MHz
There is no fixed emergency preset
items.explanation: Preset 20 is permanently programmed to the emergency frequency of 121.5 MHz, located on preset page 5 and identified by the EMER label.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-7)

items.question: Which electrical bus powers the pilot's VHF radio, and which powers the copilot's?
options: Pilot's VHF: NO. 2 DC PRI bus; Copilot's VHF: BATT bus
Both are powered by the BATT bus
Pilot's VHF: BATT bus; Copilot's VHF: NO. 1 DC PRI bus
Both are powered by the NO. 2 DC PRI bus
items.explanation: The pilot's VHF radio is powered by the NO. 2 DC PRI bus (through the PLT VHF breaker), while the copilot's VHF radio is powered by the BATT bus (through the CPLT VHF breaker) — giving the copilot's radio power even if both generators and the primary buses are lost.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-7)

items.question: How many presets are available for each of the COM, NAV, and ADF radios on the RTU?
options: Up to twenty
Up to five
Up to ten
Only one, which must be reprogrammed each flight
items.explanation: Up to twenty presets can be programmed, across five preset pages, for each of the COM, NAV, and ADF radios.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-1, I-5-3)

items.question: What happens to the RTU display if left on a main or preset page with no input for 20 seconds?
options: It automatically returns to the top-level display
It powers itself off to save the battery
It locks and requires a password to unlock
Nothing — the RTU stays on whatever page was last selected indefinitely
items.explanation: The RTU automatically returns to the top-level page after 20 seconds of inactivity on a lower-level page.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: COMMUNICATIONS (p.I-5-1)

items.question: What does the independent DME tuning function let the pilot do?
options: Select a separate DME station for distance while bearing continues to be determined relative to the original VOR station
Tune two different DME stations simultaneously and average their distances
Disable the DME entirely while keeping VOR bearing active
Automatically slave the DME to whichever VOR is nearest
items.explanation: With independent DME tuning, pressing DME-H while locked onto a VOR/DME station and then tuning to a new DME station gives distance from the new DME station while bearing information continues to come from the original VOR station.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-1)

items.question: Where is marker beacon sensitivity controlled, and what are the two settings?
options: At the ICS (audio controller) panel — MB SENS pushed in selects HI sensitivity, popped out selects LO
On the NAV main display page only, toggling between AUTO and MANUAL
On the RTU top-level page, toggling between STRONG and WEAK
Marker beacon sensitivity is fixed and cannot be adjusted
items.explanation: Marker Beacon sensitivity is controlled at the ICS (audio controller) panel: pushing MB SENS in selects HI sensitivity; pressing again to pop it out selects LO sensitivity.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-2)

items.question: What is distinctive about how the ADF-462 tunes between its two frequency bands?
options: Tuning is continuous and "wraps" seamlessly between the 190.0–1799.0 kHz and 2179.0–2185.0 kHz bands as the tuning knob is turned
The pilot must manually select which of the two bands to tune into via a separate switch
Only one band is usable in flight; the second is for ground testing only
The two bands can never both be tuned in the same flight
items.explanation: The ADF frequency is tunable in 500 Hz increments across two bands (190.0–1799.0 kHz and 2179.0–2185.0 kHz), and the tuning is configured to wrap seamlessly between the two bands as the tuning knob is adjusted.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-3)

items.question: Which ADF preset is permanently programmed to the emergency frequency, and what is that frequency?
options: Preset 20, at 2182.0 kHz
Preset 1, at 500.0 kHz
Preset 10, at 1000.0 kHz
There is no dedicated ADF emergency preset
items.explanation: ADF preset 20 is permanently programmed to the emergency frequency of 2182.0 kHz, identified by the EMER label.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-3)

items.question: Regardless of switch position, when does the transponder automatically select STBY mode?
options: When the aircraft is on the ground
Above 10,000 ft
During autorotation only
It never automatically changes mode
items.explanation: Regardless of the ON/STBY switch position, the transponder automatically selects STBY mode whenever the aircraft is on the ground.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-4)

items.question: What is the Mode A transponder code range, and how long does pressing IDENT transmit the identification signal?
options: Code range 0000–7777; IDENT transmits for 20 seconds
Code range 0000–9999; IDENT transmits for 5 seconds
Code range 0000–7777; IDENT transmits for 10 seconds
Code range 1000–7000; IDENT transmits continuously until cancelled
items.explanation: The Mode A ATC code range is 0000–7777. Pressing IDENT causes the transponder to transmit the IDENT signal for 20 seconds (note this differs from the ADF/ATC self-test duration, which is 10 seconds).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-4)

items.question: What is TCAS's normal maximum range, and how far can it exceptionally track intruders?
options: Typically 18 NM, though intruders may be seen out to 36 NM
Typically 5 NM, up to 10 NM
Typically 50 NM, up to 100 NM
TCAS range is fixed at exactly 30 NM with no variation
items.explanation: The typical maximum TCAS range is 18 NM, though there are instances where intruders may be seen out to 36 NM. TCAS can track as many as 45 aircraft and displays up to 30 of them.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-5, I-6-6)

items.question: Under what conditions does TCAS Sensitivity Level A (SL A) apply, versus Sensitivity Level B (SL B)?
options: SL A applies below 2000 ft AGL or when the landing gear is extended; SL B applies under all other flight conditions
SL A applies above 10,000 ft; SL B applies below 10,000 ft
SL A applies only on the ground; SL B applies only in flight
SL A and SL B are selected manually by the pilot at all times
items.explanation: TCAS applies Sensitivity Level A (a less sensitive TA threshold, to reduce unnecessary advisories in dense terminal-area traffic) when below 2000 ft AGL or when the landing gear is extended. Sensitivity Level B applies under all other flight conditions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-5)

items.question: What are the three TCAS display range modes, and their altitude volumes relative to own aircraft?
options: Normal (-2700 to +2700 ft), Above (-2700 to +9000 ft), Below (-9000 to +2700 ft)
Normal (-1000 to +1000 ft), Above (0 to +5000 ft), Below (-5000 to 0 ft)
There is only one fixed display mode covering ±2700 ft
Climb, Cruise, and Descent modes, selected automatically by flight phase
items.explanation: The three TCAS display modes are Normal (-2700 ft to +2700 ft), Above (-2700 ft to +9000 ft), and Below (-9000 ft to +2700 ft), determining which altitude volume of intruders is displayed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-6)

items.question: If a TCAS traffic warning triggers with no TCAS display currently selected, what happens ("pop up" mode), and how does EGPWS interact with it?
options: TCAS forces a NAV ARC page onto the center MFD first, then the pilot's inboard MFD, then the copilot's inboard MFD; an EGPWS pop-up takes precedence over a TCAS pop-up
Nothing happens automatically — the pilot must manually select the TCAS display
TCAS pop-up always overrides and blocks any EGPWS display
The pop-up only appears on the copilot's MFD, never the pilot's
items.explanation: In pop-up mode, if more than three displays are operational and none is currently showing TCAS, a traffic warning forces a NAV ARC page with TCAS onto the center MFD (if installed), then the pilot's inboard MFD, then the copilot's inboard MFD, in that order. An EGPWS pop-up display takes precedence over a TCAS pop-up.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-6)

items.question: On the TCAS traffic display, what does a filled yellow circle around an intruder symbol indicate?
options: The intruder is potentially hazardous
The intruder is a friendly/known aircraft
The intruder's transponder is not reporting altitude
The intruder is more than 20 NM away
items.explanation: A filled yellow circle around a TCAS traffic symbol indicates that intruder is potentially hazardous.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-6)

items.question: What triggers a TCAS Traffic Advisory (TA) in terms of time to Closest Point of Approach (CPA)?
options: When TCAS predicts time to CPA is between 15 and 30 seconds (depending on sensitivity level)
Only when the intruder is within 100 ft vertically, regardless of time
TAs are issued continuously for any detected transponder-equipped aircraft
Only when two intruders are detected simultaneously
items.explanation: TCAS issues a Traffic Advisory (aural "Traffic, Traffic" plus a TRAFFIC display) when it predicts a possible collision hazard — specifically when time to CPA falls between 15 and 30 seconds, with the exact threshold depending on the active sensitivity level (SL A or SL B).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-4, I-6-5)

items.question: Can TCAS detect an intruding aircraft that has no operating transponder?
options: No — TCAS is unable to detect any intruding aircraft without an operating transponder
Yes, using onboard radar independent of any transponder
Yes, but only within 1 NM range
Yes, as long as the intruder is reporting altitude via ADS-B
items.explanation: TCAS is unable to detect any intruding aircraft that does not have an operating transponder — it works by interrogating other aircraft's transponders (ATCRBS Mode A/C or Mode S).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: NAVIGATION (p.I-6-5)

items.question: Which fuel tank supplies the APU, and does the APU supply power to the buses at all times?
options: The No. 1 fuel tank supplies the APU; the APU does not supply power to the buses unless both main generators are offline
The No. 2 fuel tank supplies the APU; it always supplies power to the buses when running
The APU has its own dedicated fuel tank separate from the engines
The No. 1 fuel tank supplies the APU; it powers the buses only when on the ground
items.explanation: Fuel is supplied to the APU by the No. 1 fuel tank. The APU generator provides power to the helicopter buses on the ground (rotors not turning) and as emergency power in flight, but it does not supply the buses at all unless both main generators are offline.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-1)

items.question: What happens for four seconds after the APU CTRL switch is placed to ON, before the APU actually starts?
options: The APU runs through its built-in test (BIT)
The fuel prime pump runs alone with no other checks
Nothing — this is simply a mandatory cool-down wait unrelated to testing
The pilot must manually confirm three separate prompts
items.explanation: When the APU CTRL switch is placed to ON, there is a four-second delay while the APU goes through its built-in test (BIT) before it actually starts.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-1)

items.question: How does the ESU's response to a sensed "protective condition" differ between on the ground and in flight?
options: On the ground it causes an APU FAIL caution and automatic shutdown; in flight it only causes an APU FAULT caution, with no automatic shutdown
It behaves identically on the ground and in flight
In flight it shuts the APU down automatically; on the ground it does not
Protective conditions never cause a caution in either case, only safety conditions do
items.explanation: On the ground, the ESU treats both safety and protective conditions the same way: APU FAIL caution plus automatic shutdown. In flight, a safety condition still causes APU FAIL and automatic shutdown, but a protective condition only causes an APU FAULT caution — the ESU does not command an automatic shutdown for a protective condition in flight.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-1, I-9-2)

items.question: When the FIRE APU/ARM pushbutton is pushed, which four things happen?
options: The fire extinguisher system arms, the ESU commands an APU shutdown, the prime/APU boost pump turns off, and the APU fuel shutoff valve closes
Only the fire extinguisher discharges — nothing else changes
The APU immediately restarts to burn off residual fuel
It only illuminates a warning light with no other system action
items.explanation: Pushing FIRE APU/ARM arms the fire extinguisher system, commands the ESU to shut down the APU, turns off the prime/APU boost pump, and closes the APU fuel shutoff valve.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-2)

items.question: What pressure range does the APU accumulator operate between (fully charged vs. discharged), and at what pressure does APU ACCUM LOW illuminate?
options: 4000 psig fully charged, 2500 psig discharged; APU ACCUM LOW illuminates at 3450 psig
1000 psig fully charged, 500 psig discharged; APU ACCUM LOW illuminates at 750 psig
8000 psig fully charged, 6000 psig discharged; APU ACCUM LOW illuminates at 7000 psig
The accumulator has no low-pressure warning
items.explanation: The APU accumulator pressure gauge indicates 4000 psig fully charged and 2500 psig discharged. If accumulator pressure drops to 3450 psig, the APU ACCUM LOW advisory illuminates.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-2)

items.question: What powers the APU starter motor for engine start, and what recharges this system?
options: A nitrogen-pressurized accumulator with hydraulic fluid, recharged by the No. 3 hydraulic system (or manually via a hand pump)
A dedicated 24V battery pack recharged by the No. 1 generator
Compressed air from the ECS, recharged by engine bleed air
It uses main engine hydraulic pressure exclusively, with no backup
items.explanation: The APU accumulator (in the cabin overhead) contains pressurized nitrogen and hydraulic fluid, separated by a piston, to operate the starter motor. It's normally recharged by the No. 3 hydraulic system, with a hand pump available for manual recharge if that system is unavailable.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-2)

items.question: At what APU speed does the start valve close and the starter motor secure, and at what speed does the ignition unit secure?
options: Start valve closes / starter secures at 50%; ignition unit secures at 94.5%
Start valve closes at 10%; ignition secures at 50%
Both occur simultaneously at 100%
Start valve closes at 94.5%; ignition secures at 50%
items.explanation: During APU start: at 10% speed the fuel shutoff solenoid and ignition unit energize; at 50% speed the start valve closes and the starter motor is secured; at 94.5% the ignition unit is secured and the hour meter/start counter begin operating.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-2, I-9-3)

items.question: Besides electrical power, what other two functions does the APU provide?
options: Pneumatic power for engine starting, and heating for the cockpit and cabin
Hydraulic power for the flight controls, and fuel transfer between tanks
Rotor brake actuation, and windshield anti-ice
Only electrical power — it has no other function
items.explanation: In addition to providing electrical power, the APU supplies pneumatic power for engine starting and heating for the cockpit and cabin.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AUXILIARY POWER UNIT (p.I-9-1)

items.question: How are the engine inlets anti-iced, versus the compressor inlet guide vanes and IPS axial inlet?
options: Inlets: electrically heated dual-zone mats; guide vanes/IPS inlet: engine bleed air, metered by FADEC based on Ng and T1
Both are anti-iced by engine bleed air only
Both are anti-iced electrically, with no bleed air involved
Inlets: bleed air; guide vanes/IPS inlet: electrical heating mats
items.explanation: The engine inlets are anti-iced by electrically (AC) powered, dual-zone heating mats. The compressor inlet guide vanes and IPS axial inlet are anti-iced by engine bleed air instead, with the FADEC determining how much bleed air to route based on Ng and T1 (engine inlet temperature).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: What temperature does the inlet anti-ice controller aim to maintain the inlet surface above?
items.explanation: The inlet anti-ice controller regulates the two heating mats to ensure the inlet surface stays greater than 4°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: Under what conditions does the TRN PIT HEAT OFF caution illuminate, and what does it warn the pilot to do?
options: On the ground with Nr below 80% and any PITOT HT switch ON — warning that pitot heat should be turned off
In flight with OAT above 20°C — warning to turn pitot heat off since it's no longer needed
It illuminates continuously any time pitot heat is on, regardless of conditions
Only during engine start, to prevent pitot tube overheating
items.explanation: TRN PIT HEAT OFF illuminates when the helicopter is on the ground, Nr is below 80%, and any of the PITOT HT switches are ON — prompting the crew to turn pitot heat off since it isn't needed and unnecessarily draws power/heats the tube on the ground.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: Under what conditions does the TRN PIT HEAT ON caution illuminate?
options: In flight, OAT below 40°F (4°C), and not all three PITOT HT switches are ON
On the ground with OAT below freezing, regardless of switch position
Whenever the standby pitot heat switch alone is OFF
Only during the before-takeoff check, regardless of temperature
items.explanation: TRN PIT HEAT ON illuminates when the helicopter is in flight, OAT is below 40°F (4°C), and not all three PITOT HT switches are ON — prompting the crew to turn all pitot heat on in icing-prone conditions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: When operating on APU generator power only, what happens to the copilot's windshield anti-ice, and how can the pilot's be recovered?
options: Copilot windshield anti-ice is not available; pilot windshield anti-ice can be recovered by selecting the OVRD (override) position
Both pilot and copilot windshield anti-ice remain fully available
Neither windshield anti-ice is available under any circumstances on APU power
Only the copilot's anti-ice remains available; the pilot's is lost with no recovery option
items.explanation: On APU generator power only, copilot windshield anti-ice is not available. Pilot windshield anti-ice can be recovered by selecting the override (OVRD) position on the ANTI-ICE WDSHLD PLT switch.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: How much continuous operating time does the windshield washer reservoir provide?
options: About 2 minutes (2-quart reservoir)
About 10 minutes
About 30 seconds
It has no fixed capacity — it draws from the potable water tank
items.explanation: The windshield washer reservoir has a two-quart capacity, enough for about two minutes of continuous operation.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-2)

items.question: What main components make up the Active Vibration Control (AVC) system?
options: Ten accelerometers, an Nr sensor, an AVC computer, an Electronic Unit (EU), and three or more Force Generators (FGs)
A single accelerometer and one Force Generator
Only software running on the existing FADEC, with no dedicated hardware
Two accelerometers and a hydraulic damper
items.explanation: The AVC system uses ten accelerometers, an Nr sensor, an AVC computer, an Electronic Unit (EU), and three or more Force Generators (FGs) to detect and cancel airframe vibration.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-2)

items.question: How does a Force Generator (FG) in the AVC system actually cancel vibration?
options: It has two mechanical units with counter-rotating weights; driven exactly 180° out of phase they produce zero net force, but slightly out of that phase they produce a net force used to cancel vibration
It uses a single spinning weight that always produces a constant cancelling force
It hydraulically dampens vibration using engine oil pressure
It relies entirely on software prediction with no moving parts
items.explanation: Each FG has two mechanical units (MUs) with motor-driven concentric weights rotating in opposite directions. Driven 180° out of phase, they cancel each other's force (net zero); when slightly out of that phase, they produce a net force that's used to cancel airframe vibration.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-3)

items.question: Under what conditions is the AVC system automatically disabled?
options: When Nr is below 90%, or when both main generators are offline
Only when the aircraft is on the ground
It is never automatically disabled — only manually via its switch
When OAT is below freezing, regardless of rotor speed
items.explanation: The AVC system is automatically disabled when Nr is below 90%, or when both main generators are offline.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-3)

items.question: What is the difference between the AVC FAIL and AVC DEGRADED cautions?
options: AVC FAIL means the BIT shut the whole system down; AVC DEGRADED means it continues operating in a reduced-performance mode
They indicate the same fault, just with different display colors
AVC DEGRADED is more severe and always precedes AVC FAIL
AVC FAIL only applies on the ground; AVC DEGRADED only applies in flight
items.explanation: If the AVC computer's built-in test detects an error, it either shuts the system down (AVC FAIL caution) or continues operating in a degraded mode (AVC DEGRADED caution), depending on the severity of the fault.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-3)

items.question: In the WDSHLD WIPER switch's three positions, what does OFF do specifically (versus simply stopping the wipers wherever they are)?
options: OFF parks the wipers in the inboard position
OFF parks the wipers in the outboard position
OFF leaves the wipers wherever they happen to stop
OFF folds the wiper arms away from the glass entirely
items.explanation: When the WDSHLD WIPER switch is set to OFF, the wipers park in the inboard position (rather than stopping wherever they happen to be); SLOW and FAST select the two operating speeds.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: UTILITY SYSTEMS (p.I-10-1)

items.question: What are the five modules that make up the Main Gearbox (MGB)?
options: Two input modules, the main module, and two accessory modules
One input module, two main modules, and two accessory modules
Two input modules and three main modules
One combined module with no separate sections
items.explanation: The MGB consists of five modules: two input modules, the main module, and two accessory modules, and it has a built-in 5° forward tilt.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-1)

items.question: What does the freewheel unit in the input module allow, and what continues to be driven if an engine fails?
options: It allows the engine to disengage during autorotation or OEI operation; the accessory module continues to be driven by the MGB
It locks the engine to the rotor system permanently, preventing any disengagement
It allows the rotor brake to engage automatically on engine failure
It disengages the tail rotor drive shaft only, leaving the main rotor unaffected either way
items.explanation: The freewheel unit in the input module allows the engine to disengage from the drivetrain during autorotation or OEI (one engine inoperative) operation. If an engine fails, its accessory module continues to be driven by the MGB.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-1, I-12-2)

items.question: What triggers the LOW ROTOR light and aural warning, and how can the aural be silenced?
options: Nr below 95% with weight-on-wheels not detected; silenced by Nr recovering above 95%, landing, or pressing VOICE CNCL on the cyclic
Nr below 100% at any time, silenced only by landing
It only triggers on the ground, never in flight
It cannot be silenced except by shutting down the engines
items.explanation: If Nr drops below 95% and weight-on-wheels is not detected, the LOW ROTOR light illuminates and the aural sounds continuously until Nr increases above 95%, the helicopter lands, or the VOICE CNCL button on the cyclic is pressed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-2)

items.question: Between the two Nr sensors on the accessory modules, what does each one feed?
options: No. 1 Nr sensor feeds the DCU (cockpit display, HUMS, AVC computer); No. 2 Nr sensor feeds each engine's FADEC
Both sensors feed only the cockpit display, for redundancy
No. 1 feeds the FADEC; No. 2 feeds the DCU
Each sensor feeds only its own accessory module, with no cockpit connection
items.explanation: The No. 1 Nr sensor supplies rotor speed information to the DCU for cockpit display, HUMS, and the AVC computer, while the No. 2 Nr sensor supplies rotor speed information to each engine's FADEC.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-2)

items.question: What is the difference between the MGB OIL PRES caution and the MGB OIL PRES warning?
options: Caution: either the input manifold or last-jet pressure switch trips; Warning: both trip together, also triggering a "GEARBOX PRESSURE" aural alert
They are the same indication, just shown in different colors depending on flight phase
Caution applies in flight; warning applies only on the ground
Warning occurs first, and if uncorrected downgrades to a caution
items.explanation: If either the input manifold pressure switch or the last-jet pressure switch trips, an MGB OIL PRES caution displays. If both trip together, it escalates to an MGB OIL PRES warning with a "GEARBOX PRESSURE" aural alert.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-2, I-12-3)

items.question: What does the 30-second time-delay relay in the MGB chip detector system do?
options: Allows small chips and fuzz to burn off and/or wash away, preventing false chip warnings
Delays the entire chip detection system from arming for 30 seconds after engine start
Automatically shuts down the MGB oil pump for 30 seconds to clear debris
Delays the aural alert only, not the visual caution
items.explanation: The chip detectors are magnetic plugs that attract ferrous particles; a 30-second time-delay relay allows small chips and fuzz to burn off and/or wash away, preventing false chip warnings from trivial debris.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-3)

items.question: Why does a hot oil indication disable the chip detector's fuzz burn-off feature?
options: To prevent electrical arcing when the oil is in a vaporous state
To save electrical power during an already-abnormal condition
It doesn't disable it — fuzz burn-off always remains active
To force an immediate precautionary landing
items.explanation: A hot oil indication disables the fuzz burn-off feature to prevent electrical arcing, since the oil may be in a vaporous state at high temperature.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-3)

items.question: What does the Bearing Monitor System (BMS) monitor, and what does it illuminate if it detects an out-of-limit condition?
options: Vibration and temperature on the swashplate, tail rotor drive shaft bearings #1 and #2, and the oil cooler bearing — illuminating CHECK BMS
Only main rotor blade track and balance, illuminating TRACK FAULT
Engine oil pressure only, illuminating ENG OIL PRES
Cabin vibration levels for passenger comfort, illuminating CABIN VIB
items.explanation: The BMS processes vibration and temperature data on the swashplate, tail rotor drive shaft bearings #1 and #2, and the oil cooler bearing. Detecting an out-of-limit temperature or vibration condition illuminates the CHECK BMS advisory.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-3)

items.question: Is the rotor brake designed to stop the rotor before engine shutdown?
