options: No — it holds the rotor stationary during start and slows/stops it after shutdown, but is not designed to stop it beforehand
Yes, it is the primary means of stopping the rotor at any time, including before shutdown
It can only be used to stop the rotor in an emergency, never during normal operations
It is only used for maintenance ground runs, never in normal flight operations
items.explanation: The rotor brake holds the rotor stationary during engine start and slows/stops the rotor after engine shutdown — it is explicitly not designed to stop the rotor prior to engine shutdown.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-3, I-12-4)

items.question: How does the ROTOR BRAKE caution logic differ between being on the ground versus in the air?
options: On the ground, either the pressure switch or the puck position sensor triggers the caution; in the air, both sensors must agree to trigger it
It behaves identically in both cases
In the air, either sensor triggers it; on the ground, both must agree
The caution is completely disabled while airborne
items.explanation: Either the pressure switch or the puck position sensor illuminates the ROTOR BRAKE caution while on the ground; while in the air, both sensors must trip to illuminate the caution.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-4)

items.question: Can both engines be started with the rotor brake engaged, and what limits engine advancement in that case?
options: Yes, both engines may be started with the rotor brake on; the FADEC will not advance either engine past idle until Np is above 24%
No, the rotor brake must be fully released before any engine start is attempted
Only one engine may be started with the brake on; the second requires the brake off
The rotor brake automatically releases once engine start is initiated
items.explanation: Both engines may be started with the rotor brake on. The FADEC will not allow the engines to advance past idle until Np is above 24%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-4)

items.question: What does the Intermediate Gearbox (IGB) do, and where is it located?
options: Located at the base of the tail pylon, it transfers torque from the No. 3 to No. 4 drive shaft, changes drive direction, and reduces shaft speed
Located in the MGB itself, it has no separate function from the main module
Located at the top of the tail pylon, it drives the tail rotor directly with no speed reduction
It only provides lubrication to the tail rotor gearbox, with no torque transfer role
items.explanation: The IGB, located at the base of the tail pylon, transfers torque from the No. 3 drive shaft to the No. 4 drive shaft, changes the direction of the drive, and reduces shaft speed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-4)

items.question: When can the IGB and TGB oil level be checked using their optical liquid sensors?
options: Only on the ground with rotors not turning
At any time, in flight or on the ground
Only in flight above 500 ft AGL
Only during the power assurance check
items.explanation: The IGB and TGB each have an optical liquid sensor that detects oil level only on the ground with rotors not turning, illuminating IGB OIL LEVEL or TGB OIL LEVEL if oil is not present.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-4, I-12-5)

items.question: What does the MGB OIL BYP switch's TEST position do?
options: A momentary position that actuates the bypass valve and illuminates MGB BYPASS on EICAS, then returns to NORM when released
Permanently routes oil through the bypass valve until manually reset
Simulates a chip detection fault for crew training
Disables the MGB oil pressure alert system for maintenance
items.explanation: TEST is a momentary switch position: placing it in TEST actuates the bypass valve and illuminates MGB BYPASS on EICAS, then the switch automatically returns to NORM when released.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: POWERTRAIN (p.I-12-3)

items.question: At what Nr does the main rotor droop stops move fully outward during run-up, and what happens during shutdown?
options: Fully outward at 70–75% Nr; during shutdown, they move back into position as Nr decreases below 50%
Fully outward at 100% Nr only; they never move back into position until the rotor fully stops
Fully outward at 20% Nr; move into position below 90% Nr
Droop stops are fixed and do not move with Nr at all
items.explanation: Centrifugal force pulls the droop stops fully outward at 70–75% Nr during run-up, allowing full blade motion. During shutdown, as Nr decreases below 50%, the droop stops move back into position to limit blade droop at low/stopped rotor speed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-1)

items.question: What do the flap restraints limit at low Nr, and to what maximum flap angle is the blade allowed as Nr increases?
options: At low Nr, upward flap is limited to 0.5°; as Nr increases, full motion up to +25° maximum is allowed
At low Nr, upward flap is limited to 10°; full motion is never allowed regardless of Nr
Flap restraints only limit downward movement, not upward
The maximum flap angle is fixed at 5° regardless of Nr
items.explanation: The flap restraints and anti-flap stop limit upward blade movement (flap) to just 0.5° at low Nr; as centrifugal force increases with Nr, the restraints pull outward allowing full vertical motion up to +25° maximum.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-1)

items.question: What fluid do the main rotor blade dampers use, and how much does each contain?
options: Silicone fluid, one quart per damper
Hydraulic mineral oil, one gallon per damper
Synthetic engine oil, half a quart per damper
Dampers are dry and require no fluid
items.explanation: Each main rotor blade damper contains one quart of silicone fluid, with a fluid level rod and FULL/REFILL scale on the reservoir end to check the level.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-1)

items.question: What is the function of the "lead stop" (also called the "hunting stop") on a main rotor blade damper?
options: It prevents over-extension of the damper in the horizontal (lead/lag) axis
It stops the blade from flapping upward past its limit
It locks the damper completely during ground shutdown
It limits pitch change authority on that blade only
items.explanation: Each damper has internal stops that limit blade travel during normal operations; the lead stop (hunting stop) specifically prevents over-extension of the damper in the horizontal lead/lag axis.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-1)

items.question: What vibration does the bifilar vibration absorber cancel, and what provides its "constant tuning" across the Nr range?
options: 4-per-revolution vibrations; tuning is constant because it uses the rotating system's centrifugal force field as the restoring force
1-per-revolution vibrations; tuning is fixed mechanically and does not vary with Nr
Engine-induced vibrations only, tuned electronically by the AVC computer
It cancels all vibration frequencies indiscriminately with a passive rubber mount
items.explanation: The bifilar is a four-armed, X-shaped device with pendulum weights that cancel 4-per-revolution vibrations. Using the rotating system's centrifugal force field as the restoring force gives it constant tuning throughout the Nr range, without needing active adjustment.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-2)

items.question: What are the S-92 main rotor blades constructed from, and how many are there?
options: Four composite blades: graphite/fiberglass spar with honeycomb core, fiberglass skin, and a titanium/nickel leading-edge abrasion strip
Five aluminum-alloy blades with a steel leading edge
Two wooden-core blades wrapped in carbon fiber
Four blades made entirely of titanium
items.explanation: There are four composite main rotor blades: each has a graphite/fiberglass spar with a honeycomb core, wrapped in a fiberglass skin, with a titanium and nickel abrasion strip on the leading edge.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-2)

items.question: What is the twist of the main rotor blade from root to tip, and how are the tips shaped?
options: 13° of twist root to tip; tips are swept back, tapered, and anhedral (angled downward 20°)
0° twist (constant chord); tips are square-cut with no sweep
45° of twist; tips are dihedral (angled upward)
13° of twist; tips are straight with no sweep or anhedral
items.explanation: Each main rotor blade has 13° of twist from root to tip, with tips that are swept back, tapered, and anhedral — angled downward at 20°.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-2)

items.question: Does the S-92 tail rotor require lubrication?
options: No — it is a bearingless controllable-pitch system requiring no lubrication
Yes, it requires the same oil servicing as the tail gearbox
Only the pitch links require periodic greasing, but the blades themselves do not
Yes, via a dedicated hydraulic reservoir feeding the hub bearings
items.explanation: The tail rotor is a bearingless, controllable-pitch system that requires no lubrication.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-3)

items.question: At what angle is the tail rotor canted, and what percentage of total lift does this provide in hover?
options: Canted 20°, providing about 4% of total lift in hover
Canted 90° (perpendicular), providing no lift contribution
Canted 5°, providing about 15% of total lift
Canted 45°, providing about 25% of total lift
items.explanation: The tail rotor is canted 20°, which provides approximately 4% of the helicopter's total lift during hover operations, in addition to its directional/anti-torque function.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-3)

items.question: How do the tail rotor blades change pitch, given the tail rotor has no conventional pitch-change bearings at the blade root?
options: By twisting the flexbeam that attaches each blade to the rotor hub
Through a conventional feathering bearing at the blade root
Pitch is fixed and cannot be changed in flight
Through a swashplate identical in design to the main rotor's
items.explanation: Tail rotor pitch change and blade flap are accomplished by twisting the flexbeam that attaches each blade to the rotor hub, rather than through a conventional bearing.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-3)

items.question: What is the difference between the S/P TEMP DETECT caution and the S/P TEMP LIMIT caution for swashplate temperature?
options: S/P TEMP DETECT illuminates at 110°F above ambient temperature; S/P TEMP LIMIT illuminates when swashplate temperature exceeds an absolute 300°F
They are the same caution, just displayed at different times of flight
S/P TEMP DETECT is only active on the ground; S/P TEMP LIMIT only in flight
S/P TEMP LIMIT is a less severe indication than S/P TEMP DETECT
items.explanation: The Bearing Monitor Unit (BMU) uses two swashplate temperature sensors plus ambient temperature from the ADC. S/P TEMP DETECT illuminates when swashplate temperature is 110°F above the ambient baseline; S/P TEMP LIMIT illuminates when the absolute swashplate temperature exceeds 300°F.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-3)

items.question: What are the hub's precone and prelag angles on the S-92 main rotor head?
options: Preconed 6°, prelagged 9°
Preconed 0°, prelagged 0° (fully rigid)
Preconed 20°, prelagged 20°
Preconed 9°, prelagged 6°
items.explanation: The titanium main rotor hub is preconed 6° and prelagged 9°, with elastomeric bearings that allow the blades to lead/lag and flap.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-1)

items.question: How does the rotating swashplate transmit flight control inputs to the main rotor blades?
options: Through the pitch control links and the rotating scissors assembly to the blade retention yokes
Directly through a rigid mechanical shaft with no intermediate linkage
Via electrical actuators mounted on each blade root
Through the stationary swashplate only, bypassing the blade retention yokes entirely
items.explanation: The rotating swashplate is connected to the main rotor hub by the rotating scissors and to the blade retention yokes by adjustable pitch control links, which vary blade pitch as the swashplate tilts or moves with flight control input.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ROTOR SYSTEM (p.I-13-2)

items.question: What does the Collective-to-Pitch mixing unit coupling compensate for?
options: Changes in rotor downwash on the horizontal stabilizer caused by collective pitch changes — providing forward input to the main rotor as collective increases, aft as it decreases
Changes in torque effect from collective position changes
Rolling moments caused by changes in tail rotor thrust
The vertical thrust component of the canted tail rotor
items.explanation: Collective-to-Pitch coupling compensates for changes in rotor downwash effects on the horizontal stabilizer caused by collective changes: the mixing unit provides forward input to the main rotor as collective increases, and aft input as collective decreases.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-2)

items.question: What does the Collective-to-Yaw mixing unit coupling do as collective is increased?
options: It increases tail rotor pitch, compensating for the increased torque effect
It decreases tail rotor pitch to reduce anti-torque authority
It has no effect on tail rotor pitch, only on the horizontal stabilizer
It disengages the tail rotor servo entirely
items.explanation: Collective-to-Yaw coupling compensates for changes in torque effect caused by collective changes: the mixing unit increases tail rotor pitch as collective is increased, and decreases it as collective is decreased.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-2)

items.question: What does the Collective-to-Roll mixing unit coupling compensate for?
options: Rolling moments caused by changes in tail rotor thrust as collective is changed
Pitching moments from changes in rotor downwash on the stabilizer
Yaw moments from asymmetric engine torque
Vibration from the main rotor blades at high collective settings
items.explanation: Collective-to-Roll coupling compensates for the rolling moments caused by changes in tail rotor thrust: the mixing unit provides left lateral input to the main rotor as collective is increased, and right lateral input as collective is decreased.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-2, I-15-3)

items.question: What does the Yaw-to-Pitch mixing unit coupling compensate for?
options: The vertical thrust component of the canted tail rotor as tail rotor pitch changes
The rolling moment from tail rotor thrust changes
Rotor downwash effects on the horizontal stabilizer
Engine torque changes during OEI operation
items.explanation: Yaw-to-Pitch coupling compensates for changes in the vertical thrust component produced by the canted tail rotor as its pitch changes: the mixing unit provides aft input to the main rotor as tail rotor pitch increases, and forward input as it decreases.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-3)

items.question: What happens if one of the two tail rotor yaw control cables breaks?
options: Tail rotor control is maintained by tail rotor quadrant spring tension, triggering a TR QUAD caution and the MASTER caution
The tail rotor immediately loses all control authority
The remaining cable automatically doubles its mechanical advantage with no caution shown
The AFCS automatically takes over full yaw control with no pilot indication
items.explanation: If one of the two tail rotor control cables breaks, control is maintained by the tail rotor quadrant's spring tension, which triggers a TR QUAD caution along with the MASTER caution.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-3)

items.question: What happens if BOTH tail rotor control cables break?
options: A centering spring sets a fixed tail rotor position
The tail rotor is left completely free to flap uncontrolled
The rotor brake automatically engages
The aircraft immediately becomes uncontrollable with no fallback
items.explanation: If both tail rotor control cables break, a centering spring sets the tail rotor to a fixed position (rather than leaving it completely uncontrolled).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-3)

items.question: What function is disengaged automatically when the tail rotor pedal switches are pressed?
options: The AFCS heading hold feature
The AFCS attitude hold feature
The rotor brake
The engine anti-ice system
items.explanation: The tail rotor pedals contain switches that, when pressed, disengage the heading hold feature of the AFCS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-3)

items.question: How does a pilot adjust the tail rotor pedal leg length?
options: Pull the PED ADJ T-handle on the outboard side of the instrument panel, which unlocks the spring-loaded pedals; apply pressure to both pedals to position them, then release the handle to lock
Loosen a floor-mounted bolt on each pedal individually with a hand tool
Pedal position is fixed and cannot be adjusted in flight or on the ground
Use the AFCS control panel to electrically motor the pedals to the desired position
items.explanation: Pulling the T-handle marked PED ADJ (on the outboard side of the instrument panel) unlocks the pedals, which are spring-loaded to move toward the operator. Pressure on both pedals simultaneously positions them; releasing the handle locks them in place.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-3)

items.question: On the collective stick, what does pressing TRIM REL do, and what happens to the collective position when it's released?
options: It releases the collective stick trim; when released, the stick maintains whatever new position it was moved to
It resets the collective to a fixed neutral detent position
It disengages the collective entirely, requiring a manual reset procedure
It only works when the aircraft is on the ground
items.explanation: TRIM REL on the collective grip releases the collective stick trim; once released, the stick maintains its new (moved) position rather than snapping back.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-2)

items.question: What does the OEI SELECT control on the collective grip do?
options: Selects OEI limiter ratings
Selects between main and reserve fire bottles
Selects the active hydraulic system
Arms the emergency flotation system
items.explanation: OEI SELECT, located on the collective grip, is used to select OEI (one engine inoperative) limiter ratings.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: MECHANICAL FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.I-15-2)

items.question: Is the AFCS dual redundant in all of its features?
options: It is dual redundant in every feature except the trim actuators
It is fully dual redundant with no exceptions
Only the SAS function is redundant; everything else is single-string
The AFCS has no redundancy at all
items.explanation: The AFCS is dual redundant in all features (SAS, ATT hold, CFD) except the trim actuators, which are single.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-1)

items.question: What do the four RVDTs (Rotary Variable Differential Transformers) tell the AFCS, and why does this matter?
options: They report actual flight control position, letting the AFCS distinguish a pilot-commanded input from a gust-induced disturbance
They measure engine torque for OEI limiting
They report rotor RPM for the AVC computer
They detect ice accumulation on the flight controls
items.explanation: Four RVDTs are installed in line with the mechanical flight controls to report control position to the AFCS. This lets the AFCS differentiate between a gust-related aircraft disturbance and a pilot-commanded attitude change.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-1)

items.question: What is the key functional difference between the trim actuators and the SAS servos in terms of cockpit control movement?
options: When trim actuators move, the cockpit flight controls also move; when SAS servos move, the cockpit controls do not move
Neither ever moves the cockpit controls
Both always move the cockpit controls identically
Only SAS servos move the cockpit controls; trim actuators never do
items.explanation: When the trim actuators move, the cockpit flight controls move along with them (visible stick movement). When the SAS servos move, the cockpit controls do not move — SAS authority is applied "invisibly" between the cockpit controls and the rotor.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: How much control authority does a single SAS servo have, and how much do the two SAS servos in one axis combine to provide?
options: 5% authority per servo; 10% combined per axis
50% authority per servo; 100% combined
100% authority per servo, fully redundant
1% authority per servo; 2% combined
items.explanation: Each SAS servo can move the flight controls quickly but is limited to 5% control authority. During normal operation, the two SAS servos in each axis combine for a total of 10% control authority.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: What do the boost servos do, and does the AFCS have any input to them?
options: They act like power steering, reducing control force and limiting feedback; the AFCS has no input to the boost servos
They provide full autopilot authority and are directly commanded by the AFCS
They are only used during autorotation to lighten pedal loads
They replace the SAS servos entirely on this aircraft
items.explanation: The four hydraulic boost servos act like power steering in a car, reducing the force required to move the flight controls and limiting feedback. The AFCS has no input to the boost servos at all.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: What is the fundamental behavior of SAS (Stability Augmentation System) — does it try to return the aircraft to its original attitude after a disturbance?
options: No — SAS only provides rate damping to stop the disturbance; it does not attempt to return the aircraft to its original attitude
Yes, SAS always restores the exact pre-disturbance attitude
SAS only works below 50 KIAS and does nothing above that speed
SAS is purely a warning system with no control authority
items.explanation: SAS senses a disturbance (e.g. an uncommanded nose-up pitch from a gust) and makes small, immediate control inputs to stop it — this is rate damping. SAS does not attempt to return the aircraft to its original attitude; that is the AP's job once engaged.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: If a primary SAS computer or its sensors fail, what can the pilot select instead, and what powers it?
options: Secondary SAS, in which the AP computer (using AHRS data) controls that side's SAS servos
There is no backup — a primary SAS failure disables SAS on that side permanently
The boost servos automatically take over full SAS function
The trim actuators substitute directly for the failed SAS computer
items.explanation: If a primary SAS computer or its primary sensors are not functioning, the pilot may select secondary SAS — in this mode, the AP computer uses AHRS data to control that side's SAS servos.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: What must be engaged before the AP (autopilot) section can be engaged?
options: Primary or secondary SAS
Nothing — AP can engage independently of SAS
Both FMS units must be coupled first
The rotor brake must be released
items.explanation: Primary or secondary SAS must be engaged before the AP can be engaged, since the AP section adds attitude hold and enhancements on top of the basic SAS function.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: How does the AP's heading hold behavior change above versus below 50 KIAS?
options: Below 50 KIAS, AP provides heading hold; above 50 KIAS, it provides heading hold in level flight and turn coordination during a turn
Heading hold is only available above 50 KIAS; below that, only attitude hold works
The behavior is identical at all airspeeds
Heading hold disengages automatically above 50 KIAS with no substitute function
items.explanation: The AP provides heading hold when below 50 KIAS. Above 50 KIAS, it provides heading hold during level flight and turn coordination during a turn — both delivered through the trim actuators.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-3)

items.question: On the AFCS control panel, what is the difference between the ATT and SAS positions?
options: ATT: attitude hold and AP enhancements both function (normal mode). SAS: attitude hold is unavailable, but AP enhancements still function
They are identical settings with different labels
SAS provides more capability than ATT and is the normal mode
ATT disables the SAS servos entirely
items.explanation: When ATT is selected (the normal mode), attitude hold and AP enhancements both function. When SAS is selected instead, attitude hold is not available, but AP enhancements (like hover augmentation and gust alleviation) still function.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-5)

items.question: What happens when the COUPLE button is pushed while the aircraft is already coupled?
options: The aircraft decouples, although the CFD command bars remain visible on the PFD
It re-engages the coupled mode with a fresh reference
It has no effect while already coupled
It switches from FD1 to FD2 control
items.explanation: The COUPLE button illuminates when at least one control axis is coupled. Pushing it while coupled decouples the aircraft, though the CFD command bars will still be present on the PFD.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-5)

items.question: Which Mode Select Panel (MSP) controls which Flight Director?
options: The copilot's MSP controls the #1 Flight Director; the pilot's MSP controls the #2 Flight Director
The pilot's MSP controls the #1 Flight Director; the copilot's controls the #2
Each MSP only controls the flight director on its own side, with no cross-control
Both MSPs jointly control a single shared Flight Director
items.explanation: Somewhat counterintuitively, the copilot's MSP controls the #1 Flight Director, and the pilot's MSP controls the #2 Flight Director. The FD 1-2 button on the AFCS control panel selects which MSP is actually in control of the coupled functions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-6)

items.question: If the aircraft is banked beyond 30° in ATT mode and the trim release button is released, what does the AFCS do?
options: It automatically attempts to return the aircraft to 30° angle of bank
It holds whatever bank angle the aircraft was at, however extreme
It disengages ATT mode entirely and reverts to SAS only
It commands a full wings-level recovery to 0° bank
items.explanation: In ATT mode, if the aircraft is rolled beyond 30° angle of bank when the cyclic trim release button is released, the AFCS will automatically attempt to return the aircraft to 30° of bank rather than holding the excessive angle.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-6)

items.question: What must be turned ON for yaw pedal position hold, turn coordination, and heading hold to function?
options: The yaw trim button/actuator
The collective trim button only
Both AP1 and AP2 simultaneously
The RESET button on the AFCS control panel
items.explanation: The yaw trim button turns the yaw trim actuator on or off, and yaw trim must be ON for yaw pedal position hold, turn coordination, and heading hold to function.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-5)

items.question: What is used to provide radar altitude hold, and what other approach function does the same radar altimeter data support?
options: The radar altimeter provides height above ground for radar altitude hold, and is also used in the ILS approach deceleration and level-off functions
The ADC alone provides both radar altitude hold and ILS deceleration data
GPS altitude is used instead of a radar altimeter for both functions
Radar altitude hold and ILS deceleration are unrelated to any shared sensor
items.explanation: The radar altimeter provides height above the ground to the AFCS, used for radar altitude hold, and this same data is also part of the ILS approach deceleration and level-off functions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-2)

items.question: How does the FADEC data fed to the Coupled Flight Director (CFD) get used?
options: To limit the collective axis when coupled to altitude or vertical speed modes
To directly control cyclic trim during an ILS approach
Only for engine instrument display, with no AFCS function
To determine when to engage secondary SAS
items.explanation: The FADECs provide torque, engine temperature, Np, Ng and fuel flow information to the CFD, which is used to limit the collective axis when the aircraft is coupled to altitude or vertical speed modes — preventing the CFD from commanding more power than the engines can safely deliver.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: AFCS (p.I-16-2)

items.question: At what ejector outlet temperature, and at what cabin ejector inlet temperature, will the heating system shut down?
options: Outlet exceeding 180°F, or cabin inlet exceeding 80°F
Outlet exceeding 300°F, or cabin inlet exceeding 150°F
Only outlet temperature matters — inlet temperature has no shutdown threshold
Outlet exceeding 100°F, or cabin inlet exceeding 50°F
items.explanation: Each ejector has an overtemperature sensor that shuts the heating system down if ejector outlet temperature exceeds 180°F. The system will also shut down if cabin ejector inlet temperature exceeds 80°F.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: Why can the cockpit be heated above the normal 80°F maximum in certain situations?
options: To allow for defogging the windshield
To speed up engine warm-up on cold days
It cannot be heated above 80°F under any circumstances
Only to dry out wet avionics equipment
items.explanation: The cockpit can be heated above 80°F specifically to allow for defogging.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: With the AIR SRCE HEAT/START switch in the ENG position, where does heater bleed air actually come from?
options: Whichever of the engine or APU is providing the highest pressure bleed air at the time
Always from the engines, never the APU, regardless of pressure
Always from the APU as the default, with the engine as backup only
From a dedicated auxiliary compressor unrelated to the engines or APU
items.explanation: With the switch in the ENG position, heater bleed air comes from whichever system — engine or APU — is providing the highest pressure bleed air. In the APU position, bleed air comes only from the APU.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: Why does the heating system automatically shut down if the APU FIRE or #1 ENG FIRE warning light is on, when the APU is the bleed air source?
options: To avoid ingesting smoke or flames into the heating system
To conserve APU power for the fire extinguisher system
It's an unrelated coincidental shutdown with no specific safety purpose
To prevent overheating of the APU generator
items.explanation: When the APU is providing bleed air for heating, the heater shuts down if the APU FIRE or #1 ENG FIRE warning is on, specifically to avoid ingesting smoke or flames into the heating system and cabin/cockpit air supply.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: Does the heating system automatically shut down during an APU start, and what should the crew do about the HEAT switch beforehand?
options: It will not automatically shut down during an APU start — APU starts should not be attempted with the HEAT switch ON
It always shuts down automatically for both engine and APU starts, so switch position doesn't matter
It never shuts down for any type of start
The HEAT switch has no relationship to APU starting at all
items.explanation: The heating system will momentarily shut down during a main engine start, but it will NOT automatically shut down during an APU start — so APU starts should not be attempted with the HEAT switch in the ON position.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: What is different about aircraft prior to serial number 10 regarding APU heat?
options: They cannot use the APU as an inflight heat source
They cannot use the APU for ground heat
They have no APU-sourced heat capability at all, ground or flight
They require a longer APU warm-up before heat is available
items.explanation: Aircraft prior to serial number 10 cannot use the APU as an inflight heat source (ground use is not restricted by this note).
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: How many overhead gaspers does the air conditioning system use in the cabin versus the cockpit?
options: 18 in the cabin, 4 in the cockpit
4 in the cabin, 18 in the cockpit
10 in the cabin, 10 in the cockpit
2 in the cabin, 2 in the cockpit
items.explanation: The air conditioning system uses 18 overhead gaspers in the cabin and 4 overhead gaspers in the cockpit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-2)

items.question: What is the difference between AC mode and MAX AC mode on the air conditioning system?
options: AC mode mixes fresh air with conditioned air; MAX AC mode closes the fresh air valves and recirculates compartment air through the condensers for maximum cooling
AC mode is for the cockpit only; MAX AC is for the cabin only
They are identical, just different display labels
MAX AC only operates one of the two compressors instead of both
items.explanation: In AC mode, fresh air is mixed with conditioned air. In MAX AC mode, the fresh air valves close and compartment air is recirculated through the condensers instead, for maximum cooling.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)

items.question: How is avionics equipment cooled, and what happens if a primary cooling fan fails?
options: Each avionics compartment has a primary and backup DC-driven fan; the backup automatically takes over if the primary fails
A single fan cools all avionics racks with no backup
Avionics racks rely solely on passive airflow from the cabin ventilation system
Cooling fans are only used on the ground; in flight, ram air alone cools the avionics
items.explanation: The left/right avionics racks and center console each have a primary and backup DC-driven cooling fan; the backup automatically takes over when a primary fan failure is sensed. Each MFD also has its own dedicated cooling fan.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-2)

items.question: Can the ventilation system be used independently of the heating system?
options: Yes — the ventilation system can be used with or without the heating system on
No — ventilation only functions when heating is also selected
No — the two systems share a single combined switch with no independent options
Ventilation is only available on the ground, never in flight
items.explanation: The ventilation system can be used with or without the heating system on, drawing in fresh ambient air via separate fans and discharging it through cockpit overhead and cabin ceiling ducts.
references: S-92 RFM Part 2 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL SYSTEMS (p.I-17-1)
